findings.summary: The "4. Broken Matchers" table overflows the right page edge, truncating its second column header and every value in it.
findings.evidence: Header renders as "Attacl" (clipped "Attack") with no right border; cell values are cut to "https://app", "https://(", "https:/" and a bare "«" on the "exact string set" row.
findings.fix: Constrain the table to the right column width (wrap or shrink the attack-origin strings, or stack Check/Attack as two lines per row) so the full second column and the table's right border sit inside the content margin.

findings.summary: Row 1 has 3 cells but the table has 2 columns.
findings.fix: Add or remove cells so every row has 2.

findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, so the actual hook is buried in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of CORS FIELD NOTES. 'Failed to fetch' is almost never a fetch problem."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and move the series label later or drop it, e.g. "'Failed to fetch' is almost never a fetch problem. (Part 2 of CORS FIELD NOTES.) This 10-part field guide walks the whole CORS handshake — ..."

findings.summary: The "Server Configuration Patterns" chapter opens on its closing points — layer duplication, gateway config and filter ordering — so the reader is shown broken and advanced server setups before any correct pattern (public `*`, exact allowlist + echo + `Vary`, omit-ACAO rejection, framework snippets) has been taught.
findings.evidence: Page 1's first blocks are `{"type":"heading","text":"Layer Duplication"}` and "App adds ACAO, load balancer adds ACAO too"; the correct pattern only appears two pages later as "Safe Allowlist Shape" (page 2) and "Omitting ACAO is the correct rejection" (page 3).
findings.fix: Open page 1 with the baseline patterns first — public read-only `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (no credentials, no `Vary`), then the allowlist/echo/`Vary: Origin` shape with the omit-ACAO rejection rule and one framework snippet (Express `cors()` before auth, or the Nginx `always` note) — and keep Layer Duplication / gateway / ordering as the closing blocks of that page.

findings.summary: Chapter 9 material (reflect-any-origin, broken matchers, unescaped regex dot) is taught at the bottom of page 1 under the Server Configuration title, so page 2 — the page actually titled "Misconfigurations That Become Vulnerabilities" — begins mid-chapter without its headline vulnerability.
findings.evidence: Page 1 contains `{"type":"heading","text":"The Classic Bug","ink":"red"}` with "Blind reflection + credentials = full read of user data" and the "Broken Matchers" table, while page 2 (`page_title` "Misconfigurations That Become Vulnerabilities", no `cont` flag) opens at "Over-Trusted Origins".
findings.fix: Move "The Classic Bug", "Broken Matchers" and "The Unescaped Dot" callout to the top of page 2 so the vulnerability chapter starts with its defining bug, and backfill page 1 with the configuration patterns it currently skips.

findings.summary: The "Safe Allowlist Shape" snippet references an undeclared variable `origin`, so the recommended code throws a ReferenceError instead of emitting the header.
findings.fix: Bind the value first: `const origin = req.headers.origin` and then `if (OK.has(origin)) res.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin)`.

findings.summary: `Vary: Origin` is set only inside the allowlist-match branch, so rejected-origin responses are cached without the Vary key and can be reused for allowed origins (the exact cache-poisoning failure the part warns about).
findings.fix: Move `res.set('Vary', 'Origin')` above the `if` so every response — match or not — carries it; only ACAO stays conditional.

findings.summary: The bullet "Never return 403 that still carries CORS headers" flatly contradicts the part's own (correct) guidance to emit CORS headers on error responses.
findings.evidence: "Never return 403 that still carries CORS headers" vs. page 1 "Set CORS headers on 401/403/500 too" and page 4 "Also check the header on a 401 and a 500".
findings.fix: Rewrite as origin-scoped, e.g. "Never send CORS headers to an origin you rejected — but do send them on 401/403/500 for allowed origins."

findings.summary: The entire debugging playbook (steps 1–4) is delivered on page 3 under the misconfiguration chapter's title, and page 4 — the page titled "Debugging Playbook & Recap" — then re-teaches step 2 as if it were new, so its own chapter opener depends on an earlier page.
findings.evidence: Page 3 (`page_title` "Misconfigurations That Become Vulnerabilities (cont.)") carries "Step One: Read The Error", "Steps Two To Four" and "Reproduce with `curl -H 'Origin: ...'` explicitly"; page 4 then opens with "Reproduce Without A Browser" and a second `curl -sI ... -H 'Origin: https://app.com'` block.
findings.fix: Start the playbook on page 4: move "Step One: Read The Error", the console-message table and "Steps Two To Four" onto page 4 ahead of "Reproduce Without A Browser", and merge the duplicated curl-reproduce block into the single step-2 section; leave page 3 to finish the misconfiguration audit content.

findings.summary: The "Safe Allowlist Shape" snippet — the only worked example of the correct pattern in this part — references an undeclared `origin`, so the one implementation a learner would copy does not run.
findings.evidence: "const OK = new Set(['https://app.com'])", "if (OK.has(req.headers.origin)) {", "  res.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin)" — `origin` is never bound; the checked value is `req.headers.origin`.
findings.fix: Bind the value first: `const origin = req.headers.origin`, then `if (OK.has(origin)) { res.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin); res.set('Vary', 'Origin') }`.

findings.summary: The lead-in claim that each console message maps to exactly one fix is contradicted by the very table it introduces, whose first row lists two distinct causes.
findings.evidence: "Each message maps to exactly one fix — do not guess before reading it." followed by row ["No ACAO header is present", "never emitted, or only on 200"].
findings.fix: Soften to "Each message narrows the fix to one or two causes" (the table already enumerates them).

findings.summary: The Pattern/Verdict table has a malformed first row with three cells against two headers.
findings.fix: Drop the trailing empty string so the row is ["public read-only `*`","safest"].

findings.summary: The reproduction command uses `curl -sI`, which issues HEAD rather than GET, so it can miss or misreport the CORS headers the browser's actual GET would receive.
findings.fix: Use a real GET with headers shown: `curl -s -D - -o /dev/null https://api.com/x -H 'Origin: https://app.com'` (same for the page 3 probe).

findings.summary: The checklist states unconditionally that the preflight returns `Allow-Credentials: true`, which is wrong for the non-credentialed APIs the same checklist recommends.
findings.evidence: "Preflight also returns `Allow-Credentials: true`" immediately after "Credentials only when needed; no reflection, no regex"
findings.fix: Qualify it: "If credentials are used, the preflight must also return `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` — otherwise omit the header."

findings.summary: The closing one-liner claims CORS never decides who may ask the question, but a failed preflight does stop the actual non-simple request from ever being sent.
findings.evidence: "CORS is the server telling the browser who may read the answer — it never decides who may ask the question."
findings.fix: Scope it to simple requests, e.g. "— for simple requests it never stops the question from being asked, only the answer from being read; a failed preflight does block the request."
